chapter_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers (Bravehearts)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Reading the Letters and Building First Understanding

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.180): paired discussion on homage and ways to honour soldiers.
Let us discuss (p.187): war heroes table — contributions and awards.

time_bands.activity: Open the textbook to p.180. Ask students what the word 'homage' brings to mind, then invite two or three responses before moving to the pre-reading pair task on ways to honour soldiers.
Read Soumya's letter (p.180–186) aloud with the class following along; pause at each of the four Chakras to let students absorb the description of the memorial.
Students work in pairs to complete the war-heroes table from 'Let us discuss' (p.187), filling in contributions and awards for Lance Naik Albert Ekka and Major Padmapani Acharya.
Take whole-class feedback on the table; draw attention to the Param Vir Chakra citation and the significance of post-Independence conflicts listed on the memorial's 29,000 tablets.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate the memorial's four Chakras — a brief sketch of concentric rings on the board helps them keep Amar, Veerta, Tyag, and Raksha Chakra distinct. The war-heroes table grounds abstract patriotism in specific names and deeds, which is the letter's core pedagogical move.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for a quick concentric-ring diagram

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Ananda's Letter, Extract Analysis, and Listening to Gunjan

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.192): extract analysis — tone, everlasting flame, opinion phrases.
Let us listen (p.196): answer questions in two–three words heard from Gunjan's speech.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.192): answer questions on Ananda's letter — 'Pushp ki Abhilasha' and actions Ananda plans to take.

time_bands.activity: Read Ananda's reply letter (p.188–191) aloud; students follow the text and note Ananda's reference to 'Pushp ki Abhilasha' and Captain Anuj Nayyar.

Work through the extract-analysis questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.192–193) as a guided class discussion: the tone of Soumya's writing, what the everlasting flame suggests, and identifying Ananda's opinion phrases.

Read Gunjan's speech (p.223) aloud twice — once at normal pace, once slowly — while students note answers to the five listening questions on pp.196–197 in two or three words as instructed; take oral responses at the end.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read both letters, students can now contrast Soumya's wonder-filled description of the memorial with Ananda's reflective gratitude — this contrast is the heart of the extract-analysis discussion. For the listening task, remind students the instruction asks for exact words from the speech, not paraphrases.

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Dreaming of Professions and Building Word Power

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.197): paired turns — dream profession, reason, and required preparation.
Let us learn (p.194): prefix matching and paragraph completion using new prefix-formed words.

time_bands.activity: Students work in pairs on the speaking task (p.197): each partner names a dream profession from the picture, gives a reason, and describes the preparation needed; the teacher circulates to prompt fuller sentences and model formal register.
Brief whole-class share — two or three pairs report back; draw out the language of aspiration ('I hope to…', 'This requires…') on the board.
Introduce the prefix task from 'Let us learn' (p.194): students match prefixes to meanings and root words, then complete the soldiers' paragraph using the new words; take answers together at the end.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse the prefix meaning with the root word when coining new words — write one completed example (re- + activate = reactivate) on the board before they attempt the rest. The speaking task works best when pairs alternate roles so both students practise expressing aspiration.

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.195): divide sentences from the text into main clause and subordinate clause.
Let us learn (p.196): combine sentence pairs using subordinating conjunctions and complete open clauses.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.195): fill missing vowels to find words associated with 'brave'.

time_bands.activity: Read the four model sentences from 'Let us learn' (p.195) aloud; students identify the subordinating conjunction in each before attempting the clause-division task individually.
Students divide each sentence into its main clause and subordinate clause in writing; the teacher selects responses and discusses on the board, focusing on how the conjunction signals dependency.
Move to the combining task (p.196): students join sentence pairs using because, unless, when, where, though; then complete the open clauses; pairs compare answers before brief class correction.

periods.teacher_notes: A common difficulty is treating a sentence beginning with 'Though' as having no main clause — the examples from the letters (e.g., 'Though seriously wounded… he continued to fight') ground the grammar in a context students have already read. Students who finish early can attempt the open-clause completion independently.

periods.section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
periods.activity_title: Letter Writing and Exploring the Armed Forces

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.197): guided letter to a friend on Armed Forces' peacetime contributions.
Let us explore (p.198): read Armed Forces mottos and discuss other national forces with the teacher.

time_bands.activity: Briefly discuss the three peacetime roles of the Armed Forces named in the writing task — natural calamity relief, infrastructure development, welfare initiatives — inviting one student example for each.

Students draft their letter to a friend using the textbook prompts (p.197): they plan a greeting, three body paragraphs (one per peacetime role), and a closing; the teacher circulates to give brief formative nudges on format and register.
Two or three students read their letters aloud; the class offers one positive observation each, and the teacher highlights effective formal-letter features (date, salutation, paragraphing, sign-off).

Read the three Armed Forces mottos from 'Let us explore' (p.198) together; students suggest one or two other national forces they know (CRPF, BSF, Coast Guard), and the teacher invites them to look up further examples as self-study.

periods.teacher_notes: Students familiar with Soumya and Ananda's letter exchange can draw on that model for tone and format — the epistolary form is not new to them by this point in the chapter. Encourage specific detail in the body paragraphs: a named calamity or infrastructure project makes the letter more convincing than general claims.
materials: Lined paper or exercise books for letter drafts

items.source_lo: Student reads and analyses an informational text by retrieving specific details, interpreting authorial tone, and making inferences about purpose using an informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Two letters between Soumya and Ananda about the National War Memorial, its four Chakras, war heroes Albert Ekka and Padmapani Acharya, and collective civic gratitude.
items.item_stem: Soumya describes four concentric Chakras at the National War Memorial. Read the following descriptions and match each Chakra in Column A with its correct feature in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A — Chakra | Column B — Feature
Amar Chakra | Six bronze battle murals
Veerta Chakra | Eternal flame (Amar Jawan Jyoti) at the centre
Tyag Chakra | Trees representing soldiers guarding the nation
Raksha Chakra | Granite tablets with soldiers' names etched in gold

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Amar Chakra — Eternal flame (Amar Jawan Jyoti) at the centre; Veerta Chakra — Six bronze battle murals; Tyag Chakra — Granite tablets with soldiers' names etched in gold; Raksha Chakra — Trees representing soldiers guarding the nation.

answer_key.right: Eternal flame (Amar Jawan Jyoti) at the centre
Granite tablets with soldiers' names etched in gold
Trees representing soldiers guarding the nation

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student reads and analyses an informational text by retrieving specific details, interpreting authorial tone, and making inferences about purpose using an informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Two letters between Soumya and Ananda about the National War Memorial, its four Chakras, war heroes Albert Ekka and Padmapani Acharya, and collective civic gratitude.
items.item_stem: Both Soumya and Ananda write their letters with strong emotion — Soumya moves from wonder to tears and resolve, while Ananda responds with reflective gratitude. What does the exchange of these two letters suggest about the authors' shared purpose in writing to each other? Use evidence from both letters in your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Both letters show that Soumya and Ananda write to deepen each other's sense of civic duty and gratitude toward soldiers; Soumya shares direct experience of the memorial to move Ananda emotionally, while Ananda responds by connecting it to literature and community action, suggesting their shared purpose is to inspire each other to honour the soldiers' sacrifice in concrete ways.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student listens to a spoken monologue and retrieves key information accurately, distinguishing stated reasons from personal opinion using a listening text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Gunjan's speech on why she wishes to join the Indian Armed Forces — discipline, uniform, honour, adventure, and values taught.
items.item_stem: Listen to Gunjan's speech about joining the Indian Armed Forces. According to Gunjan, which of the following best describes what wearing the uniform represents to her?

options.label: A
options.text: A symbol of adventure and travel

options.label: B
options.text: Hard work, pride, and a desire to serve India

options.label: C
options.text: A way to stay physically fit through training

options.label: D
options.text: An opportunity to meet new challenges every day

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the 'new experiences and adventures everyday' reason with the specific meaning Gunjan attaches to wearing the uniform.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates the benefit of regular exercise and training with the symbolic meaning of the uniform itself.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Picks up Gunjan's third reason (new challenges) and misattributes it to what the uniform represents.

items.source_section_title: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
items.source_lo: Student listens to a spoken monologue and retrieves key information accurately, distinguishing stated reasons from personal opinion using a listening text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Gunjan's speech on why she wishes to join the Indian Armed Forces — discipline, uniform, honour, adventure, and values taught.
items.item_stem: In her speech, Gunjan gives three distinct reasons for wanting to join the Armed Forces. Identify the three reasons and explain which of them reflects a personal opinion rather than a factual claim about the Armed Forces.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Gunjan's three reasons are: (1) serving the country is the most honourable job; (2) the Armed Forces instil discipline that keeps mind and body active; (3) each day brings new experiences and adventures that help one grow. The first reason — that serving the country is the most honourable job — is a personal opinion, as it expresses Gunjan's own value judgement rather than a verifiable fact.

items.item_stem: Write a complete informal letter to a friend describing how the Indian Armed Forces contribute during peacetime. Cover at least two of the following: natural calamity relief (floods, earthquakes), infrastructure development (building bridges in remote areas), and welfare initiatives (medical camps, libraries). Use correct letter format, organise your ideas in paragraphs, and conclude with a reflection on why these contributions matter.

items.source_lo: Student builds vocabulary through prefix word-formation and applies understanding of subordinating conjunctions to analyse and produce complex sentences using the section's language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Prefixes (re-, mal-, un-, anti-, extra-, ex-, de-) applied to soldier-related vocabulary; subordinating conjunctions (when, because, though, so that, unless, where) drawn from the letters.
items.item_stem: The sentence below is adapted from the chapter's theme. Identify the main clause and the subordinate clause, name the subordinating conjunction, and explain in one sentence what relationship the conjunction establishes between the two clauses. Sentence: 'Though seriously wounded in the encounter, Lance Naik Albert Ekka (wounded) continued to fight alongside his comrades so that his unit could capture the objective.'

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Main clause: 'Lance Naik Albert Ekka continued to fight alongside his comrades'; subordinate clause: 'Though seriously wounded in the encounter' (concessive) and 'so that his unit could capture the objective' (purpose). The conjunction 'though' signals a concessive relationship — the action happened despite an obstacle — while 'so that' signals purpose, showing the goal of the action.

items.source_context: Armed Forces mottos of the Army, Air Force and Navy; other national forces such as CRPF; discussion of their role and significance.
items.item_stem: The chapter mentions three Armed Forces mottos: the Indian Army's 'Sevā Paramo Dharmaḥ' (Service Before Self), the Indian Air Force's 'Nabhaḥ Spṛśaṁ Dīptam' (Touch the Sky with Glory), and the Indian Navy's 'Sham No Varunah' (Be Auspicious Unto Us Oh Varuna). Choose one motto, explain its meaning in your own words, and write a short paragraph (five to seven sentences) describing how this motto connects to the theme of sacrifice and service explored in the letters between Soumya and Ananda.

expected_elements: Accurately states the meaning of the chosen motto in own words.
Connects the motto's values to the letters' themes of sacrifice and gratitude.
Refers to at least one specific detail from the chapter (a hero, a Chakra, or a war).
Writes in organised, coherent sentences with a clear concluding thought.

items.source_lo: Student extends understanding beyond the text by researching real-world institutions and connecting them to the chapter's theme using hands-on exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Armed Forces mottos of the Army, Air Force and Navy; other national forces such as CRPF; discussion of their role and significance.
items.item_stem: Ananda mentions in her letter that she plans to create a collage of inspiring lives with her classmates. Design a project plan for a class collage titled 'Forces That Guard Our Nation'. Your plan must name at least three national forces (including at least one beyond the Army, Navy and Air Force), describe one contribution of each, and explain how the collage will be organised so that a viewer understands each force's role at a glance.

expected_elements: Names at least three forces, including one paramilitary or coast guard force.
Describes one specific contribution per named force.
Explains a clear organisational principle for the collage (e.g., one panel per force).
Connects the project's purpose to honouring service, echoing the chapter's theme.
